Mara took the last train because it was the only one left, and because the alternative was the waiting room, and because the waiting room had begun to feel like a place that wanted to keep her.

The carriage emptied stop by stop. By the time the lights of the town were gone there was one other passenger, a woman in a grey coat who read a newspaper with no date on it and never turned the page.

"You get off at the next one," the woman said, without looking up.

"I don't think there is a next one."

"There always is," she said. "That's the trouble with it."

***

The train slowed at a platform lit by a single lamp, and the doors opened onto cold air that smelled of rain and iron. There was no sign. There was no name on anything. Mara stood in the doorway with her bag against her chest and listened, and what she heard was the town she had left, very far away, still going on without her.

She stayed on the train.
